extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, theatre critics, and informed readers interested in stagecraft and comic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and staging tragedies and comedies (what to show or hide onstage, how to elicit pity/laughter, and which theatrical artifices are appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of children to elicit compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: A disconsolate Mother, with a Child in her Hand, has frequently drawn Compassion from the Audience; some modern writers escalate this by placing multiple children onstage to double or triple the distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against multiplying such incidents: introducing more children can move an audience at first but quickly becomes ridiculous when overused. The passage gives the progressive examples (one child → a princess with two children → a playwright using three → a widow with half a dozen) as an anti-pattern showing how a beautiful incident in good hands becomes ridiculous in bad ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid delighting in onstage brutal murders (public bloodshed)
rubrics_metrics.description: To delight in seeing Men stabbed, poysoned, racked, or impaled, is certainly the Sign of a cruel Temper; strewing the stage with carcasses in the last scene is odd and exposes us to contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay condemns frequent onstage butchery (an English tendency contrasted with French restraint) as absurd and barbarous. As a rule, dramatists should avoid gratuitous displays of gore which degrade taste and invite criticism of bloodlust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transact murders and executions offstage where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Murders and Executions are always transacted behind the Scenes in the French Theatre; the ancients often executed dreadful resolutions behind the scenes—e.g., Orestes's matricide is heard, not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the ancients and Horace, parricides and 'unnatural Murthers' should be withheld from public view and reported or heard offstage. The text argues such offstage execution preserves decency and is often more affecting (the behind-the-scenes dialogue between mother and son in Orestes is cited as more moving than an onstage murder).

rubrics_metrics.name: When necessary, tell rather than show shocking acts
rubrics_metrics.description: If any thing could extenuate so brutal an Action, it would be the doing of it on a sudden, before the Sentiments of Nature... However, to avoid publick Blood-shed... the Fact ought not to have been represented, but to have been told, if there was any Occasion for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an act is so brutal that its onstage depiction would be indecent or improbable, report it through dialogue or offstage sounds rather than staging the violent moment itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: If killing is avoided onstage, produce corpses afterward to preserve melancholy
rubrics_metrics.description: Though devoted Persons were seldom slain before the Audience, their Bodies were often produced after their Death, which has always in it something melancholy or terrifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compromise: perform the murderous act offstage but show the corpse onstage later to achieve the emotional effect (melancholy/terror) without indecency or improbability of onstage slaughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improbable or unnatural stage actions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indeed very odd, to see our Stage strowed with Carcasses... killing before the Audience... appears very unnatural, and looks like killing in cold Blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging actions that violate probable human behaviour (e.g., calm, deliberative murders onstage) undermines verisimilitude and audience sympathy; prefer means that maintain natural sentiment and probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Horace's rule with balance (forbear extreme horrors publicly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's Rule: forbearing to commit Parricides or unnatural Murthers before the Audience; Horace never designed to banish all Kinds of Death from the Stage, but only those with too much Horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret the rule to mean absolute prohibition of death onstage; rather, exclude only those deaths whose horror would be better effect when transacted offstage. The French over-refinement (never showing deaths) risks absurdity; the English excess risks barbarity—seek a middle way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject trivial or ignorant dramatic inventions that cheapen tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Several Dramatick Inventions are made use of by the Ignorant Poets to supply the Place of Tragedy... some of which I could wish entirely rejected, and the rest to be used with Caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful writers improve tragedy through appropriate incidents; avoid cheap artifices and contrivances (examples elsewhere in the essay: overreliance on children, grotesque stage devices) that substitute for genuine tragic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy allows broader licence: use costume and props as character shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Ridicule is not so delicate as Compassion... there is a much greater Latitude for comick than tragick Artifices... Bullock in a short Coat, and Norris in a long one, seldom fail of this Effect... in ordinary Comedies, a broad and a narrow brim'd Hat are different Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic writing and staging can rely more on visual shorthand (costume, hats, barrels, whiskers) and broad physical signs to generate laughs; these artifices are more indulgible than in tragedy. The essay lists many accepted comic devices and stresses their permissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the psychology of laughter (superiority theory) when crafting comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbs: 'The Passion of Laughter is... sudden Glory arising from some sudden Conception of some Eminency in ourselves by Comparison with the Infirmity of others...' Every one laughs at Somebody in an inferior State of Folly to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic material should exploit the audience's comparative pleasure—present characters or situations that make the audience feel superior (fools, butts, staged blunders). Different audiences require different classes of 'fools' (e.g., 'Jack Puddings' vs. higher, circumferaneous wits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create effective conversational 'butts' with wit and vivacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man is not qualified for a Butt, who has not a good deal of Wit and Vivacity, even in the ridiculous side of his Character. A stupid Butt is only fit for the Conversation of ordinary People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sophisticated audiences, the comic 'butt' should be lively and resourceful—able to give play to wits and sometimes turn ridicule back on attackers (Falstaff cited as an exemplar). Selecting the right kind of butt for the audience is essential.
